Count TriPrimes With an Optional Partial-Sieve Cutoff

triPrimeCount.Rd

Count positive integers less than or equal to \(n\) with exactly three prime factors, counted with multiplicity, excluding the first \(a\) primes as factors. This is the correction term \(P_3(n, a)\) used in Lehmer prime counting. Its table requirements impose an additional input-dependent limit described below.

Usage

triPrimeCount(n, a = 0, nThreads = NULL)

Arguments

n

A single nonnegative whole number, at most \(2^{53} - 1\). The additional table limit in ‘Details’ may restrict the accepted value for a given a. With the default a = 0, the largest accepted n is 379,625,063.

a

A single nonnegative whole number, at most \(2^{53} - 1\). This is the number of initial primes excluded as factors, not a prime value. The default, a = 0, permits every prime. For example, a = 1 excludes the prime 2, so only odd triprimes are counted. Larger cutoffs can permit larger n within the table limit.

nThreads

Requested number of threads. The default is NULL for serial execution. Requests are capped by the available hardware and the useful work in the calculation. Small or simple cases may use fewer threads. This argument is validated even when the result is immediate.

Details

Logical inputs FALSE and TRUE are converted to 0 and 1, respectively. The thread count must be positive, so nThreads = FALSE is not supported.

Mathematical definition

Let \(p_i\) denote the \(i\)th prime. The function counts products \(p_i p_j p_k \le n\) with \(a < i \le j \le k\). Nondecreasing factor order counts each integer once. Factors need not be distinct: prime cubes \(p^3\) and products \(p^2 q\) are included, as are products of three different primes.

When \(a = 0\), the excluded set is empty; no zeroth prime is needed. The seven triprimes at most 30 are 8, 12, 18, 20, 27, 28, 30. For example, 8 qualifies as \(2^3\), while 16 does not qualify because \(2^4\) has four prime factors counted with multiplicity. Excluding 2 leaves only 27 among these seven values.

Write \(\pi(t)\) for the number of primes at most \(t\), and define $$c = \pi(\lfloor n^{1/3} \rfloor), \qquad b_i = \pi(\lfloor \sqrt{n / p_i} \rfloor).$$ The smallest factor has index at most \(c\); for that factor, the middle factor has index at most \(b_i\). Once these two factors are fixed, the largest factor has index from \(j\) through \(\pi(\lfloor n / (p_i p_j) \rfloor)\). Hence, $$P_3(n, a) = \sum_{i=a+1}^{c} \sum_{j=i}^{b_i} \left[\pi(\lfloor n / (p_i p_j) \rfloor) - j + 1\right].$$ A sum with no terms is zero. In particular, the answer is zero for \(n < 8\) or \(a \ge c\): the smallest permitted prime cube then exceeds \(n\).

Relation to prime counting

At Lehmer's cutoff \(a = \pi(\lfloor n^{1/4} \rfloor)\), the surviving composites have two or three permitted prime factors. For \(n \ge 1\), $$\pi(n) = \Phi(n, a) + a - 1 - P_2(n, a) - P_3(n, a).$$ The other terms are available through primePhi and semiPrimeCount. See primeCount for the complete counting methods.

Table limit and memory use

The implementation first prepares tables through \(\lfloor n^{1/3} \rfloor\) to determine whether any qualifying triples exist. If they do, let \(p_{a+1}\) be the smallest permitted prime. Direct prime-count lookups require a table through $$q_{\max} = \lfloor n / p_{a+1}^2 \rfloor.$$ Every queried quotient is at most this value. The largest supported table limit is 94,906,265; a nonempty calculation requiring a larger table raises an error before that larger table is allocated. An empty count does not require this second table.

With a = 0, the smallest permitted prime is 2, so the condition is \(\lfloor n / 4 \rfloor \le 94906265\). This explains the default upper limit \(379625063\). Excluding more primes can reduce the required table size and allow larger inputs, up to the common numeric limit \(2^{53} - 1\) when the table condition is met.

Table storage is proportional to \(\max(n^{1/3}, n / p_{a+1}^2)\) for nonempty calculations. The dense prime-count entries alone use \(4(L + 1)\) bytes for limit \(L\), about 362 MiB at the maximum. This excludes prime vectors, temporary tables, worker storage, allocation overhead, and any shared Phi cache retained from other calls; it is not a peak-memory bound. Workers within one call share the prepared lookup tables. Inputs below the enforced table limit can still be expensive in time or memory.

Value

A single whole number giving \(P_3(n, a)\). The result has type integer when it is at most .Machine$integer.max, and type double otherwise. The count is exact for accepted inputs.

Author

Joseph Wood

See also

primePhi, semiPrimeCount, primeCount, primeSieve

Examples

## Count all triprimes, then exclude 2 as a factor
triPrimeCount(30)    ## 7
#> [1] 7
triPrimeCount(30, 1) ## 1, from 3 * 3 * 3
#> [1] 1

## Repeated prime factors are included
triPrimeCount(8)      ## 1, from 2 * 2 * 2
#> [1] 1
triPrimeCount(7)      ## 0
#> [1] 0
triPrimeCount(0)      ## 0
#> [1] 0
triPrimeCount(30, 100) ## 0
#> [1] 0

## Keep exploration modest: the default table extends through floor(n / 4)
triPrimeCount(10^5, nThreads = 2)
#> [1] 25556
